doc.title: Ellis Marsalis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Ornette, Los Angeles and the Marines
title: Disliking Los Angeles: beatniks, Lenny Bruce and club scene
summary: He explains why L.A. did not suit him and recalls Cosmo Alley, Sammy Davis, Basie and others.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: I did. I didn’t really like L.A.
Why not? What was it about L.A. that you didn’t like?
It had nothing to do with it. Music, not the music I wanted to play.
What year was this, by the way?

’58. See, rhythm-and-blues was just beginning to come to Los Angeles. Earl Palmer, who was a great drummer, he did all of the sessions here. He went to Los Angeles. He left here and went up to L.A. I would see Earl every now and then while I was in the military. The studios had guys who were used to playing studio music, backing Sinatra and all of them – the Hollywood types. There was a whole cultural change that was going on. Hollywood, all the clubs were frequently by stars, all of a sudden started to get the long-haired hippie-looking people, who had money in their pocket, but they weren’t the stars per se. All of that started to change. I remember I started – I read in the newspaper, in the L.A. Times, about the beatniks, and I’m saying, “Beatniks. I wonder what that is?” They said, in the paper, they said it was beatniks and Cosmo Alley. So I say, okay, I’m going to go check out Cosmo Alley. I went down to L.A. and went over to Cosmo Alley. It was a real small place. When I went inside, there’s all these people sitting there, suit and tie. There’s a comedian on the stage with a suit and tie, telling jokes, and I’m saying, this don’t look like no beatniks, not what they had described. Anyway, the comedian on the stage was Lenny Bruce. When I left that club, I started to think about some of them people that I was hanging out with, and I realized that that was the beatniks, turning the t.v. sound down, putting records on, sitting on a log stretched out into the living room. I said man, man, Jesus, the beatniks. It was a very interesting time for me in L.A., because when I’d go downtown – I ran into Sammy Davis one time. He was telling me about putting up the SRO sign around the corner at the Moulin Rouge. Basie was playing at the Crescendo at the time. MJQ was also playing at a different time, but it was so noisy in there, John Lewis got upset. Told them, said, “Just be quiet.” There was people like Tom Lehrer and – what’s this guy’s name? He was really funny too. He’s another comedian. He used to go – he used to read the New York Times every day and formulate his whole routine off of the newspaper. It was a very interesting time to be in L.A. Mort Saul, that’s him. He used to work one of the clubs downtown. I was only there for two years, and then I got out in December of ’57. That’s when it was. I got out in December of ’57, because I went in in – no, wait a minute, wait a minute, no.
It would be ’58, because you said you went in in January of ’57, I think.
Yeah, I did. I went in in January of ’57, and I got out in December of ’58. I had a ’56 Buick, and I drove it home.
